content:
Over decades of regular trips to Europe, Regine Rousseau, the Chicago-based founder of wine marketing and events consultancy Shall We Wine, never really subscribed to the directive often preached by U.S. travel publications: When traveling abroad, try not to let your American show.

“Number one: I like wearing really bright colors, so I rarely blend in anywhere,” says Rousseau, also senior sales advisor at Verve Wine Chicago. “Number two, I am Black, and typically when I’m traveling, I am one of few Black people, even in the places I visit in Europe. So typically they look at me and know I’m American.”

Having known what it is to be othered, this Haitian-American prefers to understand a bit of the culture she’s in rather than insert herself. With time and miles, she’s learned she’d prefer lingering over cramming in as many stops as possible. Though she’s a 70-30 wine-to-cocktail drinker, she often lets her curiosity and the environment lead her drinking choices. Thus, as a first timer in bars in Portugal and Ischia, she probably asked the bartender, “What’s your specialty?” or “What is it you make that no one else makes better than you?”

“When I’m traveling, I want to sit, I want to think, I want to have a conversation, and I really want the place to become part of me and hopefully leave something in the place I’m visiting,” Rousseau says.

Her words exude the sensibility of a seasoned traveler: One doesn’t have to fake blending in to be a good visitor.

Historically, the American Tourist has conjured some silly, occasionally unfortunate tropes: shouty, bald-faced enthusiasm through the lens of American exceptionalism. Fanny packs crammed with cash tips deposited in excess regardless of local customs. Athleisure! A penchant for vodka and ice, not to mention the trails of takeaway coffee cups we leave in our wake. We’re boisterous and opinionated, occasionally overly friendly. This shows up in our drinking behavior, too — the way we demand our Martinis just so and willingly chat up strangers at the bar. Occasionally, our exceptionalism crops up in our very American cocktail requests (Skinny Bitch, anyone?).

But with experience — nowadays Americans globetrot much more — there seems to be promise that the American tourist will embrace more of the local and the unfamiliar. Or, at least, fake it convincingly enough.

The Tenacious Martini Tourist

Over the past decade, international travel among U.S. tourists surged roughly 71 percent, per data from the International Trade Administration. In 2025, Americans took a record 24 million trips to Europe, a number that’s expected to climb by another 5 percent by the end of this year, according to The Wall Street Journal. Does all that extra mileage translate to shedding certain stereotypes as Americans descend on the drinking establishments of Madrid, London, and Rome? European bartenders say the thread connecting U.S. travelers in 2026 is largely one of curiosity and openness … though we still love our vodka.

“What can I say? Americans at the bar are entertaining, in a positive way,” says Giorgio Bargiani, assistant director of mixology at The Connaught Bar in London. Maybe he has to say that; after all, North Americans are the majority demographic at this luxury cocktail bar and its iconic namesake hotel. Bargiani can pick out U.S. visitors right away by how they engage staff and fellow customers.

“It starts when they arrive at the bar and you treat them as everybody else,” he says, “but straight away there’s conversation. There’s no shyness. There is always interest that, in my eyes, feels genuine, compared to other cultures where this interest is not necessarily false, but more polite than genuine.”

The interactions tend to spread beyond customer and bartender, until the whole bar seems to percolate with chatter about what everyone ordered and whether they like it. Of course, with gabby confidence comes opinions, of which Americans seem to proffer many, and often, about what’s in the glass. At Connaught Bar this holds especially true for Martinis, which are its bread and butter, to the tune of 30,000 made each year.

“When I moved to London [in 2014], I could see the average American guest coming in with a very precise idea of how they like their Martinis, for instance —” most notably with vodka over gin.

The same goes for ordering Martinis garnished with blue cheese-stuffed olives, as U.S. customers have been known to ask of Arturo Burzio, head mixologist at the luxury Madrid hotel Rosewood Villa Magna. (Hey, Northern Spain makes great blue cheese, right?)

“Every time you land somewhere in Italy, someone says, ‘let’s have a Spritz.’ It’s like, why? Of course, I’ll do it out of love and to participate.”

The complaint that a good Martini is hard to find is a common refrain among Americans in Europe. No matter that across much of the E.U., a “cocktail” more often refers to “something fruity, sweet, and sour” — we seem determined to believe that the savory, boozy, very American drink is a widely shared cultural touchstone.

Chalk it up to the glut of choice that pervades consumerist American culture, but we also seem to love customizing even the most classic cocktails. That the traditional Margarita contains no added sugar doesn’t stop U.S. customers requesting the cocktail be made “without sugar,” nodding to the sweeter versions commonplace around the U.S., Burzio says. He is likewise accustomed to fielding American requests for U.S. spirit substitutions, like bourbon and specific vodka brands, plus the occasional ask for American-born concoctions, like the Cosmopolitan, Vodka Cranberry, and, regrettably, the aforementioned Skinny Bitch — made with vodka, lime juice, and soda water.

You Can Take the Tourist out of America…

You can’t always take the American out of the tourist. Even the well-traveled among us occasionally give ourselves away by ordering exactly what we want, regardless of the place or its legendary status.

The historic, recently reopened cafe, cocktail bar and restaurant Bar della Pace, a stone’s throw from Rome’s Piazza Navona, is best known for spritzes, Bellinis, and Rossinis served with a side of potato chips and people watching. Some American visitors happily comply with ordering these customary aperitivi; but just as many may request a Martini or Espresso Martini, per director and manager Maria Iemma.

“They’re always friendly, cheerful and respectful,” Iemma says, wryly adding, it helps that they tip so generously.

By comparison, old hand U.S. travelers are more comfortable exploring unfamiliar ingredients and local spirits. “They may ask for recommendations, describe the flavors they enjoy, and let the bartender guide them,” Burzio notes.

They even come around to gin Martinis, Bargiani says, “because when in London, we drink gin Martinis.”

Rousseau has markedly evolved in how she travels since she first visited France as a senior in college and was horrified to learn that “cooked” steak could still be bloody inside. Most notably, she says, she’s become more of a participant than a consumer of other cultures. After all, the joy of rituals lies in experiencing them as intended.

She still recalls sitting at a bar in Porto on her first trip to Portugal and asking the bartender, “What’s interesting that is truly Porto?” Then boom! Out came that honeyed, low-ABV white port and tonic, “and it was Porto.” She drinks them whenever she is back in Portugal’s second-largest city.

She could, however, do without the sugared, sunset-colored Aperol Spritz altogether, though she can’t seem to escape it.

“Every time you land somewhere in Italy, someone says, ‘let’s have a Spritz.’ It’s like, why? Of course, I’ll do it out of love and to participate.”

When in Rome, right?

Drink the place. It’s a simple mantra that bears repeating, as our shrinking globe brings more of the world to our fingertips without the benefit of context. If Warren Johnson, the well-traveled partner at Saint Urban’s in Charleston, S.C., had stuck with his preferred beverage order of wine while visiting Antwerp, Belgium, this summer, he might have missed out on Westmalle Dubbel, the iconic reddish-brown ale made by Trappist monks just north of the city. Fortunately, he followed the local advice, and changed just a little in the process.

“Its complex, deeply bitter, fruity, and herbaceous notes seriously hit the mark,” Johnson recalls, “and with that, I’m now a beer drinker.”

content:
Gin was somewhat of a tough sell in the early days of the craft cocktail revival. Consumers were more reluctant to dive into the botanical booze like they had for brown spirits. This sometimes compelled bartenders who embraced gin to hatch creative ways to promote the category. In one legendary story, for instance, a member of Pegu Club’s roster of acclaimed bartenders would sell guests on gin by telling them it was juniper-flavored vodka.

A couple of decades later, and the gin category has blossomed into a fascinating space that virtually demands exploration from the spirits enthusiast. This is partially due to an abundance of expressions from around the world, many of which create innovative ways to build flavor around gin’s required juniper berries.

The level of choice can admittedly cause analysis paralysis among gin newcomers. Finding the right bottle to kick off a personal gin journey can be tough. Having a trusted guide that understands gin can reduce some of the difficulty, and there may not be a better font of knowledge to draw from than a bar professional. With that in mind, we asked 15 bartenders to highlight their choice for the gin that’s perfect for beginners.

Best gin for beginners, according to bartenders:

  • Bayab Orange and Marula Gin
  • Citadelle Gin
  • Fords Gin
  • Aria Classic Dry Gin
  • Condesa Gin ‘Clásica’
  • Bluecoat American Dry Gin
  • Suntory Roku Gin
  • Beefeater London Dry Gin
  • Hendrick’s Gin
  • Bayab Palm & Pineapple
  • Drumshanbo Gunpowder Gin
  • Tanqueray
  • Letherbee Gin
  • Nolet’s Silver Dry Gin
  • The Botanist Islay Dry Gin

“Bayab Orange and Marula gin distilled in South Africa is an excellent introduction for those that may find gin to be medicinal in flavor. Marula is a sub-Saharan fruit that truly represents the place where it grows: bright, vibrant, and intense. This helps allow the gin to make a great dry Martini and a great Gimlet; which is not always the case. Having the juniper and spice play a more minor role than the citrus is what sets this gin apart from the rest.” —Zack Atzert, head bartender, The Fountain Inn, Washington, D.C.

“For something right down the middle, I would go with Citadelle Gin. It’s a very approachable London style gin. It’s super easy-drinking with a wonderful punchy juniper that isn’t overpowering. They are also one of the only global gin brands to harvest and cultivate their own juniper, so they have very fresh botanicals.” —Jarett Karlsberg, beverage director, Wythe Hotel, Brooklyn

“Fords Gin is approachable for beginners because it’s balanced rather than juniper-heavy, so it doesn’t hit you with that ‘pine tree’ intensity some gins have. It was developed with input from bartenders to be versatile, meaning it works well in almost any classic cocktail. This makes it a good all-purpose bottle to learn how to make gin-based drinks. It’s also reasonably priced and widely available, so it’s an easy, low-risk way to start exploring gin.” —Charlotte Marshall, beverage director, Nic & Junior’s Tavern, Chicago

“A strong, juniper-forward flavor may not be what beginners are looking for. With that in mind, Aria Classic Dry Gin strikes a beautiful balance between the traditional London Dry style and approachable floral and citrus notes. It has layers of flavor that stand alone well in a dry Martini but also integrate perfectly into any classic gin cocktail. My summer go-to is an Aria Gin & Tonic, garnished with a fresh lime and a sprig of thyme. However, with winter right around the corner, I will soon be reaching for a classic Aria Negroni.” —Jessica Brown, bar director, Nostrana, Portland, Ore.

“One of my favorite gins for beginners, and in general, is Condesa Gin ‘Clásica.’ Condesa’s prioritization of Mexican botanicals over traditional ones found in London Dry gins such as palo santo and Mexican sage make it more palatable to someone new to gin, while making it softer on the palate. Its versatility is also a major plus; we love using it in White Negronis and Martinis alike.” —Ricky Dolinsky, beverage director, Dandelion and Keepers, New York City

“Bluecoat American Dry Gin is my no-brainer recommendation for anyone new to gin. Wonderfully textured and citrus-forward, it carries a subtle sweetness followed by a delicate, spicy finish. At 47 percent ABV, it’s dangerously sippable. From a practicality standpoint, Bluecoat is easygoing in a Martini, delightful in a Negroni, and resilient in just about any shaken cocktail.” —B. Cole, Head Bartender, Valerie, NYC

“Suntory Roku Gin is a great choice for anyone new to the world of gin. It’s expressive and approachable, showcasing delicate Japanese botanicals like sakura, yuzu, and sencha tea. Roku has significant floral and citrusy character without relying on the juniper-forward flavor that can be overwhelming for those new to drinking gin. It’s also a team player in cocktails, as its balanced profile blends harmoniously with other ingredients.” —Martha Davis, lead bartender, The Marigold Club, Houston

“Gin is a fantastic spirit. It comes in all shapes and sizes, so it is approachable for many different palates. For someone trying gin for the first time, I’d recommend a citrus-forward, London Dry style, and Beefeater London Dry Gin immediately comes to mind. It is crisp and clean, and true to its name, finishes dry. Also, If tonic is your mixer when you’re getting into gin, please make sure you’re using a great one. It matters.” —Sarah Clark, director of operations, The Dearborn, Chicago

“For someone new to gin, I would recommend Hendrick’s Gin. It is approachable without losing the character that makes gin unique. It has a smooth and easy-to-drink flavor, with light notes of cucumber and rose that make it less strong and traditional than some other gins. It also works well in simple cocktails like a Gin & Tonic, Martini, or Tom Collins. I think it is a good starting point because you can enjoy it on its own, but it also mixes well with different flavors.” —Kelly Duong, general manager and mixologist, Kyojin, Washington, D.C.

“For someone newer to gin, I think Bayab Palm & Pineapple is a really approachable entry point. The first thing you get is this bright, tropical pineapple character rather than being hit immediately with a ton of juniper. There’s still enough dryness, citrus, and botanical structure underneath it that it drinks like gin, but it gives you a familiar flavor to enter through. It’s a good example of how flavored gin can bring something very recognizable to a cocktail while still doing the job you need the gin to do.” —Kyle Jackson, beverage director, The Argyle, NYC

“I think people new to gin often have the misconception that it’s overly piney — like drinking a Christmas tree in a glass — or that it’s something their grandma drank. But there are plenty of gins that are much more approachable for beginners. Drumshanbo Gunpowder Gin, for example, is citrus- and tea-driven, with gentle spice notes that make it really enjoyable. For something even more familiar, Hendrick’s leans into cucumber and rose, creating a softer, more approachable profile. Both are great introductions to gin because they showcase its versatility without overwhelming someone who may not be accustomed to its distinctive botanicals.” —Daniel Navarro, lead bartender, CHICA, Las Vegas

“Starting off with a classic London Dry gin like Beefeater or Tanqueray is a great way to understand the category. These are classic styles where you can clearly identify the botanicals, especially juniper, along with citrus, coriander and other herbs and spices. Once you understand that classic profile, you can move into Japanese, Italian, Mexican, or small-distillery gins that use botanicals and ingredients that represent where they come from.” —José Maria Dondé Rangel, beverage director, The Bedford and Mexi, NYC

“Letherbee Gin is a versatile choice, ideal for beginners looking to craft a wide variety of cocktails. Because Letherbee does not chill-filter its gin, it retains all the rich essential oils extracted from botanicals like juniper, citrus, and aniseed. When mixed with water or other liquids, these oils bloom and create a distinct cloudy appearance, releasing an intense aroma that elevates classics like the Gin Martini or Gimlet. Additionally, Letherbee’s high proof, robust spice profile, and citrus notes allow it to complement citrus-forward drinks without being overshadowed by sugar or acid. This makes it an exceptional base for sour-style cocktails such as the Bee’s Knees, Gimlet, or Last Word. Really, it’s a great all-around gin for any bar.” —Andrew Thompson, beverage manager, Dicey’s Pizza &Tavern, Chicago

“For someone just getting into gin, I always recommend Nolet’s Silver Dry Gin because it’s beautifully floral and fruit-forward, with notes of rose, peach, and raspberry that make it softer and more approachable. I personally love it in a Gimlet because it’s bright, refreshing, dangerously crushable, and really showcases the beautiful complexity that a gin can possess.” —Jennifer Yim, master mixologist, Bellagio, Las Vegas

“To me, the classic starter gin is going to be a London dry gin. But if you want to go for a more botanical, citrusy forward gin, I would recommend The Botanist Islay Dry Gin. This gin really pushes botanical flavors, but does so without any added flavors or additives. It also makes a great Gin & Tonic.” —Galen Maclennan, beverage and general manager, Ferguson’s Country, Brooklyn

When Cody Pruitt opened Libertine, the acclaim was immediate. The restaurant became one of the hardest reservations in New York, with the fan-favorite saucisse-purée quickly taking on a life of its own.

But three years later, the initial fervor had faded, and filling the dining room every night was no longer as easy as it once had been. Pruitt made the difficult decision to close Libertine and transform the space into a new concept: Capitaine. Drawing on both the successes and shortcomings of Libertine, he set out to create a restaurant that would be easier for regulars to return to again and again.

On this episode of “The Buildout,” Pruitt joins Adam to discuss what he learned from Libertine and how he arrived at the tough decision to start over.

title: Vinitaly.USA Is Bringing 2,500 Italian Wines to New York This October
summary:

content:
Take a palatal tour from the ancient volcanic sands of Campania to the quiet medieval town of Montefalco to the high Alpine foothills of Piedmont. Taste the expressive fruit and earth notes of a Barolo (the King of Wines), the complex nuttiness of an aged white Pecorino, the bright minerality of a Prosecco from the hills north of Venice, or the luxurious full body of Amarone della Valpolicella from Veneto. You can taste all of these expressions and more without ever leaving New York City. 

On October 26 and 27, Vinitaly.USA will return for its third edition, and its first in New York. Organized in collaboration with the Italian Trade Agency, the event will bring 300 Italian wine exhibitors, and roughly 2,500 labels, to Manhattan’s Pier 36. The 11,000 square meter space will host more than 600 wine buyers and hundreds of enthusiasts, sommeliers, and journalists. Between the business sessions, masterclasses, regional collectives and wineries, there will be plenty to occupy even the most seasoned of Italian wine connoisseurs.

An Extra-Large Taste of Italy

The event’s lineup is full of exhibitors representing a wide range of regions and consortia including Asti DOCG, Brunello di Montalcino, Emilia-Romagna, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Lazio, Lugana DOC, Prosecco DOC, Sardinia, Vini delle Venezie DOC, and Vini dell’Elba.

For attendees, the options are endless – not just when it comes to a chance to taste the wines themselves, but also when it comes to the choice of approach. Spend the day on a full tour of Italian wine by hopping between regions, tasting the variations between coastal, volcanic, and mountainous regions. Or, pick a particular region or grape and follow that thread through the tasting floor. 

Take A Deeper Dive

The Italian wine landscape is famously complex, and 2,500 labels might feel a bit daunting, in theory. But at the event, there will be opportunities for a little guidance through navigating it all. For instance, the event’s educational program includes the sessions “Sardegna: An Island Apart,” on Sardinia’s island identity, and “More than Meets the Vines: Metodo Classico Today,” on the traditional Italian winemaking method. A session called “Beyond Nebbiolo & Sangiovese” will highlight the Italian grapes that don’t always get the attention they deserve, which could appeal to sommeliers looking for distinctive additions to their wine lists. Other seminars include “Worth the Wait? Italy’s White Wines and the Case for Collecting” and “Italy’s Regional Character: Award-Winning Quality With a Sense of Place.”

There’s even a chance to put your tasting instincts to the test in “Can You Taste Italy Blind?”The tasting, in which attendees have no prior knowledge of what’s in the glass, is designed to explore how different tasting frameworks approach grape recognition, regional identity, structure, and typicity. More refined than a “name that wine” party trick, the tasting will examine how to actually make sense of what’s in the glass. 

Friuli-Venezia Giulia, a northeastern region that’s home to the Dolomites and known for world-class white wines, gets a strong showing across the program. One session, titled “On the Border: Sauvignon, Ramato, and the Wines That Defy Expectations,” looks at wines from Friuli’s eastern edge, where Italy meets Slovenia. “The Lagoon Road: Friuli Venezia Giulia, from the Adriatic to the Marl of the Hills” examines the differences between Pinot Grigio from the plains versus the hills. Another session heads toward the Prealps, exploring altitude, extreme conditions, and the region’s sweeter side (“At the Edge of the Alps”).

The Business of Wine

For all the tasting, Vinitaly.USA is ultimately a trade event. The wine2wine Business Forum gives the two-day program a practical edge.

These sessions will tackle questions that are less about what’s in the bottle, and more about what happens after it leaves the winery. “The Future of Wine Tourism in Italy: Who Decides Where American Wine Travelers Go Next?” explores how Americans choose which Italian wine destinations to visit. “Italian Producers and America’s Master Sommeliers Ask Each Other the Questions That Matter” investigates how sommeliers influence wine lists. “Texas Is Not One Wine Market” zooms in on the differences between wine cultures in Austin, Dallas and Houston, while “From Importer to Shelf” takes a closer look at how Italian wines actually make their way through America’s three-tier distribution system.

That last subject may sound somewhat less romantic than a dialogue on native grapes in Sardinia, but for producers hoping to expand their presence in the U.S., it’s a valuable component of the show. For those who really want to get into the weeds, or into the vines, the final afternoon offers perhaps the most serious tasting of the program. On October 27, Master of Wine Sarah Heller will lead the two-hour Vinitaly International Academy Advanced Tasting Sessions featuring 22 wines to be tasted in comparative flights,open to Italian wine ambassadors and experts “ready to refine the way they taste, read and discuss Italian wine.”

There’s also the less structured, but no less valuable, business of meeting people. With more than 600 importers, distributors, and buyers already registered, the event is built around making connections as much as tasting wine.

Ultimately, Vinitaly.USA will showcase the fact that “Italian wine” is not so much a single category as it is a complex collection of wildly different grapes, regions, climates, traditions, and drinking cultures. You’ll leave the experience with new favourite wines to seek out, new questions to ask and a thirst to keep exploring. Click here to register today.

content:
On Wednesday, The 50, formerly known as 50 Best, announced its highly anticipated annual list of the World’s 50 Best Bars. At this year’s live ceremony in Milan, Hong Kong’s Bar Leone defended its crown as the No. 1 bar in the world, after making waves as the first bar in Asia to claim the top spot in 2025.

Italian bartender Lorenzo Antinori opened Bar Leone in June 2023, bringing the essence of Rome’s traditional neighborhood bars to Hong Kong through classic aperitivo drinks.

In the No. 2 spot is Moebius Milano, climbing up from the No. 7 position last year — an exciting feat for locals celebrating at the event in Milan. Rounding out the top five is Alquímico in Cartagena (No. 3), Bar Us in Bangkok (No. 4), and Line in Athens (No. 5).

The U.S. secured four placements on the top 50 list (down from five in 2025), all of which are based in New York City. The highest ranking U.S. bar is schmuck. — which took home VinePair’s Next Wave Award for Bar Program of the year in 2025 — in the No. 11 spot. The list also includes Sip & Guzzle (No. 16), Martiny’s (No. 46), and Bar Snack (No. 49).

title: 10 Bottles From Mexico to Try Beyond Tequila and Mezcal
summary:
Mexico’s magic is indisputable. From its ancient ruins and colorful cities to its extraordinary food, art, music, and landscapes, the country has an uncanny ability to inspire creativity. And when it comes to Mexico’s best-known spirits, tequila and mezcal still reign supreme. But they’re only two pieces of a much larger drinking culture that includes everything from ancient beverages like pulque and tepache, niche agave spirits like bacanora and raicilla, or even wildcards like sotol and pox. Given the country’s sheer diversity of creative influences, it’s no surprise that the world has become increasingly fascinated by what Mexico is pouring.

The article 10 Bottles From Mexico to Try Beyond Tequila and Mezcal appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Mexico’s magic is indisputable. From its ancient ruins and colorful cities to its extraordinary food, art, music, and landscapes, the country has an uncanny ability to inspire creativity. And when it comes to Mexico’s best-known spirits, tequila and mezcal still reign supreme. But they’re only two pieces of a much larger drinking culture that includes everything from ancient beverages like pulque and tepache, niche agave spirits like bacanora and raicilla, or even wildcards like sotol and pox.

Given the country’s sheer diversity of creative influences, it’s no surprise that the world has become increasingly fascinated by what Mexico is pouring. “Mexico has some of the most incredible distilling traditions, ingredients, and producers in the world,” Gabe Ford, bar director at Austin’s Modern Bar, says. “And what is being produced is often rooted in a deep history and culture.”

Spotlighting what’s coming out of Mexico’s beverage scene gives a sense of just how much more there is to discover beyond tequila and mezcal. From Oaxacan whiskey made with ancient corn varietals to sake brewed on Sinaloa’s coast, here are 10 Mexican-made bottles that offer a taste of the country’s impressive drinking culture.

Condesa Clásica Gin

A bottle that’s become increasingly familiar on backbars everywhere, Condesa Gin has exploded in popularity. Inspired by the Condesa neighborhood and made in Mexico City, the extra-dry style gin comes from an all-female team of distillers and celebrates many of the botanicals used in Mexican spiritual rituals and ceremonies. “Herbs like palo santo, sage, myrrh, and jasmine work beautifully with the juniper and coriander to push forward a bright, floral bouquet and a palate rich in herbal intensity and citrus zest,” Evan Flynn, bar manager of Death & Co Denver, says of the spirit. Flynn loves to swap Condesa in classics like Gimlets, Negronis, and Martinis.

Alma Finca Orange Liqueur

Without orange liqueur, there is no true Margarita, and yet French-born brands like Cointreau and Grand Marnier have long led the category. Alma Finca saw an opportunity to change that, creating a Mexican orange liqueur with a blend of bitter and sweet oranges, citrus leaves, allspice, and achiote from the Yucatán Peninsula. According to Alexandra Purcaru, co-founder and beverage director at Selva Bar in Oaxaca, these nuances yield a complex, and slightly spicier liqueur.

Primo Aperitivo

While aperitivo culture is most often associated with Italy, Mexican producers are eagerly putting their own spin on the category. Made in Mexico City, Primo combines grapefruit, hibiscus, guajillo chile, and cacao with bitter roots, herbs, and other botanicals sourced from across the country. “I love that it isn’t too sweet,” Ford says. “It has enough bitterness and structure to be super versatile behind the bar.” Try it in a spritz, or swap for another bitter aperitivo to add complexity to a familiar cocktail.

NAMI Tokubetsu Junmai Sake

Recognized as Mexico’s first premium sake, the team behind NAMI found inspiration in the similarities between their home base of Culiacán and Japan, from their shared maritime cultures to traditions of artisanal craftsmanship. The team spent years learning the traditional brewing process from a Japanese toji (master sake brewer), ultimately deciding to exclusively use Yamada-nishiki rice, widely considered the premier rice for brewing sake. At Denver’s Mezcaleria Alma, chef Johnny Curiel likes pouring Tokubetsu Junmai alongside crudo, taking the familiar sake-and-sushi pairing and applying it to Mexican seafood.

Uruapan Charanda Blanco Rum

Mexico’s relationship with sugarcane runs deep, even if rum gets far less attention than tequila and mezcal. In Michoacán, sugarcane juice, molasses, and piloncillo are used to make Charanda, a protected Mexican spirit with its own Denomination of Origin. Ford recommends adding a bottle of Uruapan Charanda Blanco to your home bar, which combines equal parts estate-grown cane juice and column-distilled molasses.

Maíz Nation Blanco Whiskey

Corn plays an incredibly important role in Mexican culture, making Maíz Nation’s decision to build a whiskey around ancient corn varietals feel especially celebratory. Distilled from four native corns sourced directly from small farmers, the unaged Blanco bottling puts the character of the grain front and center. Purcaru loves using this spirit in cocktails and also appreciates Maíz Nation’s commitment to sustainable sourcing and production, from working directly with generational farming families to operating a solar-powered, off-the-grid distillery.

Alambique Serrano Cartier 30 Oaxacan Rum

The Krassel family has been distilling aguardiente in Oaxaca since the 1930s. Three generations later, the family behind Alambique Serrano is still distilling in the high-altitude region of Santa María Tlalixtac, where they make Cartier 30 from 100 percent organic Java sugarcane and fresh cane juice. Getting to the distillery still requires a four-hour trek on an unpaved road, meaning a bottle of Cartier 30 has quite the journey behind it. Naturally fermented and bottled at 70.3 percent ABV, enjoy it neat to experience its funky, grassy character, or follow chef Curiel’s lead and use it as the base for a delicious Daiquiri.

Parejo Bienvenido Fernández Sotol Cedrosanum

Despite becoming more familiar to Mexican bar menus, sotol is still regularly mistaken for an agave spirit. Distilled from Dasylirion, a desert plant native to northern Mexico, Parejo takes its name from a term vinateros use to describe great sotol. Curiel became such a fan that his restaurants created a custom mash with the brand, named Fonda Fina, which he says tastes like the forest. If you can’t make it to one of Curiel’s restaurants, grab a bottle of Parejo’s Bienvenido Fernández, made from wild cedrosanum harvested in high-elevation Durango.

Edénico Eau de Vie ‘Mango’

Edénico’s Mango Eau de Vie is made with Creole and Petacón mangos grown in Oaxaca’s Cuicatlán Valley, fermented and twice distilled before resting in glass for a year. The spirit — included on VinePair’s 50 Best Spirits of 2023 list — delivers sweet, ripe tropical fruit notes with the true essence of mango. Edénico also produces other eau de vie from fruits like guava, plantain, prickly pear, and guanabana.

Casa D’Aristi Xtabentún

One can’t talk about Mexico without Maya culture, and Xtabentún is steeped in it. Named for a native flower, the honey and anise liqueur is inspired by balché, an ancient beverage traditionally associated with Maya ceremonies. Casa D’Aristi’s recipe dates to the 1930s, blending fermented honey from the Xtabentún flower with Mexican rum and anise. While it can be a tad sweet on its own, use it in mezcal or tequila cocktails to add a distinct depth of flavor.

title: The 30 Best Rye Whiskeys to Drink in 2026
summary:
Every year, with every new list of the best rye whiskeys, every booze writer out there tries to convince you that this (this!) is finally rye’s time to shine again. By now the story is well-told without much new to add: Rye used to be cool! Rye used to be what Americans drank in the 18th century and early 19th when East Coast-based farmer/distillers mainly only had rye grains to work with. Then Prohibition! Suddenly the thousands of tiny rye distillers in the country were whittled down to less than a dozen, and bourbon became the ubiquitous whiskey in America.

content:
Every year, with every new list of the best rye whiskeys, every booze writer out there tries to convince you that this (this!) is finally rye’s time to shine again.

By now the story is well-told without much new to add:

Rye used to be cool! Rye used to be what Americans drank in the 18th century and early 19th when East Coast-based farmer/distillers mainly only had rye grains to work with.

Then Prohibition! Suddenly the thousands of tiny rye distillers in the country were whittled down to less than a dozen, and bourbon became the ubiquitous whiskey in America.

A lifeline! The craft cocktail renaissance of the 21st century had bartenders discovering that many classics were once made with rye, not bourbon. This led to distilleries both old and new to once again begin distilling rye.

And yet, here we are in 2026 and rye whiskey has mostly remained the domain of the cognoscenti, never fully breaking into the mainstream.

We aren’t here to tell you that this (this!) is the year that is finally going to change. No, but today rye has, at the least, firmly reclaimed a place in the country — a tasty little niche for those in the know. It’s never going to be omnipresent like bourbon, never going to be glorified like Scotch, certainly never obsessed over like Japanese whisky, but…if you’re willing to explore it, you’ll find a category with an incredible breadth of flavors, spicy and bold, grainy and herbal, fruity and oaky.

Below, there are ryes from upstart bottlers, farm producers, and even a now shuttered distillery, ones finished in rum and peach whiskey barrels and with Tiger Nut added (?), plenty made with 95/5s mash bills, and tons of high-scorers from the biggest names still delivering on their legacies.

Here are the 30 best rye whiskeys to buy and drink right now.

Table of Contents

  • Why You Should Trust VinePair
  • How We Taste
  • How We Compiled This List
  • The 30 Best Rye Whiskeys to Drink in 2026
  • The Best All-Rounder Rye Whiskey
  • The Best Rye Whiskey for Cocktails
  • The Best Rye Whiskey to Seek Out and Splurge On
  • The Spiciest Rye Whiskey
  • The Best of the Rest
  • The Best Rye Whiskeys Under $50
  • The Best Rye Whiskeys Under $100
  • The Best Rye Whiskeys Over $100
  • FAQs

Why You Should Trust VinePair

Throughout the year, VinePair conducts dozens of tastings for our Buy This Booze product roundups, highlighting the best bottles across the world’s most popular wine and spirits categories.

As part of this work, VinePair’s tasting and editorial staff samples thousands of bottles every year. This helps us keep a finger on the pulse of what’s new and exciting. Crucially, it also provides us with the context needed to distinguish the simply good from the truly great — whether from a quality or value-for-money perspective, or both.

Ultimately, our mission is to offer a clear, reliable source of information for drinkers, providing an overview applicable to day-to-day buying and drinking. Learn more about VinePair’s tastings and reviews department here.

How We Taste

We believe in tasting all products as our readers typically would: with full knowledge of the producer and — importantly — price. Our tastings are therefore not conducted blind.

For this rye whiskey roundup, all expressions were sampled in Glencairn glasses and allowed to rest for a few minutes prior to tasting. We then evaluated the aromas, flavors, texture, and finish of each whiskey. Unless there was something notably off or worrying about a whiskey’s appearance — and on this occasion we encountered no such examples — we did not evaluate the products from a visual perspective.

How We Compiled the List

In order to provide our readers with the most comprehensive and thoroughly tested list of the best rye whiskeys to buy, VinePair invited producers, distributors, and PR firms working on their behalf to send samples for consideration. These bottles were submitted free of charge — producers didn’t pay to submit nor did VinePair pay for the products. All were requested with the clear understanding that submission does not guarantee inclusion in the final list.

Not only would such an agreement contradict our editorial ethics and samples policy, it simply wouldn’t be possible to include everything we received. For this rye whiskey roundup, we tasted over 70 new submissions and also retasted several bottles that were either sent to VinePair throughout the year for consideration or that had ranked highly in prior iterations of this list.

During tasting, we assigned a score to each product on a 100-point scale based on the quality and intensity of its aromas, flavors, texture, and finish. Then we reviewed all scores and compiled an editorially driven list that meets our criteria of 30 best rye whiskeys to buy right now. It’s important to note that these are not the 30 highest-scoring ryes we tasted this year. Instead, this list showcases the best bottles across every price and for every scenario — because while price is completely objective, “affordability” is not.

The 30 Best Rye Whiskeys to Drink in 2026

The Best All-Rounder Rye Whiskey

Old Overholt Extra Aged Cask Strength 11 Year Rye (2026 Edition)

The most famous brand name in American rye was overhauled in 2020 and a series of squat bottle limited editions have been released over the last several years. Beginning with 2023’s Old Overholt Cask Strength 10 Year Rye, the brand has released a new cask strength edition each year, with varying age statements (usually between 10 and 12 years) and proof (of course). This year’s edition was put into barrels in the fall of 2014 and bottled this summer at 125.6 proof. There is the classic Jim Beam peanut note on the nose backed by charred oak and spice. The palate is a well-balanced mix of spicy and sweet, coffee cake, cinnamon candy, stone fruit, leather, and an intense oaky finish. Incredibly drinkable at such a high proof, there are few flaws to be found here and much to love, whether you’re a longtime rye drinker or new to the category. Though three digits in price, it’s worth every penny.

Average price: $110
Rating: 96

See Review

The Best Rye Whiskey for Cocktails

NULU Hazelbaker Reserve Rye

This Louisville company uses 95/5 rye contract distilled by Green River Distilling Co. With that iconic mash bill it’s easy to think you’re tasting archetypal MGP whiskey — it’s herbal and dill-y, there’s a candied ginger zip of spice, but there are also sweet notes of crème brûlée and tropical fruits. At 100 proof and a friendly price, it’s ideal for classic cocktails, though perfectly fine for neat-sippin’.

Average price: $35
Rating: 93

See Review

The Best Rye Whiskey to Seek Out and Splurge On

Preservation Distillery Very Olde St. Nick Ancient Cask Rye Whiskey: Faith + Conviction

Very Olde St. Nick probably deserves a quick thumbnail history: originally created in 1986 by Marci Palatella as luxury releases of sourced, well-aged whiskey for the Japanese marketplace, by the 2010s the brand had gone dormant. In 2020, Palatella would revive the label with a series of limited edition, small batch special releases that have become cult favorites among the American whiskey intelligentsia. This eight year old Indiana rye (from undisclosed distilleries) is oddly not labeled “straight,” and the lofty nomenclature doesn’t exactly have a story to match. “What is an ‘ancient cask’?” “Why is it ‘Faith + Conviction?” Who cares? This is quite good and unique in profile. The nose is packed with berries and dark fruits while the palate leans more towards dried fruits — raisins, prunes, apricots — and just a hint of baking spices. There’s a strong Nutella note in the mid-palate with this robust whiskey moving toward a leathery, woody finish.

Average price: $210
Rating: 93

See Review

The Spiciest Rye Whiskey

Brucato Spirits Crane Cove Rye

This is the first whiskey from a California producer that has long focused strictly on amaro. Perhaps that’s why they made a rye that is so incredibly herbal and spicy. This is a blend of just two barrels of 100 percent straight malted rye whiskey distilled in 2017 at Anchor Distilling (home of our #1 rye whiskey of 2025…then later shuttered earlier this year). This 110 proof rye has bite! It’s bursting with a nose of pine, allspice, and ginger leading to a palate that has a distinct Dr. Pepper note that is incredibly delicious.

Average price: $99
Rating: 93

See Review

The Best of the Rest

The Best Rye Whiskeys Under $50

Rye & Sons Straight Rye Whiskey (2024 Vintage)

Typically, when a whiskey is priced this reasonably, the offering is packaged with a minimal proof and flavor profile. Not here with this rye from celebrated sommelier, winemaker, and restaurateur André Mack’s brand. Distilled at Castle & Key and bottled by Pinhook Bourbon (more on both, in a sec), this 97.5 proof, high-rye offering gives notes of stone fruit, peppermint, anise seed, allspice, with a peppery finish.

Average price: $29
Rating: 92

See Review

Pinhook 2026 Straight Rye

This year’s vintage from the growing brand is, yet again, distilled at Castle & Key Distillery based on the brand’s custom mash bill. It’s a bold yet drinkable rye, with mint and dill notes backed by caramel, brown sugar, and a lingering oaky finish. Great in cocktails like a Sazerac or Vieux Carré.

Average price: $38
Rating: 92

See Review

Basil Hayden Golden Rye

A rye whiskey for those folks who think Tabasco is “too spicy.” All kidding aside, this low-proof, 100 percent malted rye Jim Beam product is indeed mild and delicate, but there’s a lot to like. Floral with vanilla notes, the palate is coffee cake with a pleasantly sweet finish. Like most Basil Hayden releases, this is a great place for beginners to dip their toes into the category.

Average price: $37
Rating: 91

See Review

1792 Straight Rye

Coming out of Sazerac’s “other” distillery — Barton 1792 — this is every bit as good as the more ballyhooed ryes from Buffalo Trace. There’s no age statement (though it’s at least four years old) but there’s plenty of maturity here. There’s baking spices and some herbal dill notes, caramel and vanilla, some malty hints, and toasted oak — it’s archetypal Kentucky rye and, at 100 proof, punchy enough for cocktails.

Average price: $40
Rating: 93

See Review

New Riff Bottled-in-Bond Rye

It’s always a treat (and a challenge) when we get to the New Riff portion of our rye tastings as this Northern Kentucky brand might be making the best, and certainly most varied rye releases in the country. And yet, despite the company entering everything from 8 year old ryes to malted ryes to even sherry-finished ryes (among others), we found their most basic (and most affordable) rye the best this year. Also made with that iconic 95/5 mash bill, aged for four years in toasted and charred oak barrels, and bottled non-chill filtered, there tons of toffee and vanilla notes on the palate backed by cinnamon, black pepper, citrus zest, and wood.

Average price: $40
Rating: 93

See Review

Michter’s US★1 Single Barrel Straight Rye Whiskey

Michter’s always delivers and this year’s single barrel rye release proves that. There’s a bright, citrusy nose with plenty of baking spice; the palate leans toward butterscotch, barrel spice, and black pepper. Though a mere 84.8 proof, it still has enough oomph for cocktails but likewise works as an economical, easy-drinking neat pour.

Average price: $45
Rating: 94

See Review

Sazerac Full Proof Rye Whiskey

Though most whiskey fans like Sazerac Rye, the biggest gripe has long been that it doesn’t have a high enough proof and disappears in cocktails. No longer. This 125 “full proof” heater came out earlier in the year and it completely brings it. Though 51 percent “barely rye,” it has an incredible intensity, with baking spice, dill, and herbal notes with a sweet, caramel balance leading to a peppery, oaky finish.

Average price: $45
Rating: 94

See Review

The Best Rye Whiskeys Under $100

Chattanooga Whiskey Straight Rye Malt Whiskey

At 99 proof, this malt-forward rye (featuring three different maltings: pale, caramel, and chocolate) is surprisingly bready and a bit savory, with notes of Italian roast espresso, Starburst candies, focaccia, and a spicy, green pepper finish.

Average price: $52
Rating: 92

See Review

Second Impression Spirits NW Rye

This debut release for Second Impression Spirits takes a high-corn Maryland-style rye that was distilled in Wisconsin and ages it for its final five years of maturity in Seattle. Like Brucato, this comes courtesy of amaro makers and damn if it, too, isn’t a very herbal, medicinal-like rye that is well-rounded in mouthfeel, rich on the palate, and quite appealing.

Average price: $57
Rating: 92

See Review

Ampersand Vinea

While not exactly a rye according to the U.S. government, we’re going to let it slide because we like what master distiller Chip Tate is doing too much. Coming out of Nevada, this is a unique blend of 75 percent 8-year-old rye and 25 percent Cognac-finished 9-year-old grain neutral spirit. It sounds odd, but it somehow works. It is not surprisingly fruity, with lots of grape and orchard fruit notes. But there’s a ton of spice as well, both from the rye and French oak finishing casks.

Average price: $59
Rating: 92

See Review

Sagamore Whiskey Bottled in Bond 8-Year-Old Straight Rye

This Maryland-style straight rye is produced from two mash bills distilled, aged, and bottled in the state. The age statement and higher proof are quite welcome compared to their (still very good) Small Batch Rye. There’s a spicy, medicinal aroma — Benadryl perhaps? — with a palate of stone fruit, cherry cola, and Werther’s Originals. The bonded proof and flavor profile would work wonders in a Manhattan.

Average price: $59
Rating: 92

See Review

Redwood Empire Emerald Giant Cask Strength

This blend of four to seven year old ryes checks in with a mash bill of 92 percent rye and a bottling proof of 115.4, making for a quite spicy, though hardly one-note whiskey. The nose is citrusy with a touch of cinnamon, while the palate offers a certain hot toddy note — you can really taste the rye grains. Adding a touch of water calms down the heat, though true spice lovers will want this neat.

Average price: $60
Rating: 93

See Review

Oaklore North Carolina Straight Rye Whiskey

Produced solely from rye distilled and aged in North Carolina and at least seven years old, this is an almost rustic rye, with grainy, vegetal notes, some dirt and minerality, all balanced by a sweet, peppery finish.

Average price: $60
Rating: 92

See Review

Cedar Ridge Nine and Three Quarters

The interesting name is actually just an age statement — this Iowa distilled rye was aged for nine years and nine months. A high rye (85 percent) high-malted mash bill gives this an almost Scotch-like flavor profile, biscuity and bready with some unexpected sherry notes.

Average price: $60
Rating: 90

See Review

Wild Turkey Rare Breed Rye

With Rare Breed you’re essentially getting special edition quality whiskey that’s easy-to-find and at a great price. Another example of “barely rye” (51 percent), the barrel proof strength still keeps it hot and spicy. It’s woody on the palate, caramel and vanilla with some Honey Nut Cheerios, and a long lingering baking spice note.

Average price: $69
Rating: 92

See Review

Still Austin Single Barrel Cask Strength Rye (“Nancy’s Pick” – July 2026)

Each month, famed master blender Nancy Fraley selects a top cask-strength barrel for release only at the Austin distillery. This July “pick” is tropical and extremely spicy. The nose offers toasted coconut and salted caramel, while the palate moves toward pineapple, mangoes, and cinnamon spice. Extraordinary stuff and there’s a reason certain bottles have soared on the secondary market.

Average price: $75
Rating: 94

See Review

Joseph Magnus 10 Year Cask Strength Rye Whiskey

This new release from the venerable Michigan brand is their first ever rye. Another 95 percent rye, bottled at a smoking 113.4 proof, this whiskey has a spicy, citrusy, almost perfume-y nose. The palate is Heath bar backed by notes of cloves, black pepper, cinnamon, and a warming, tannic presence on the finish.

Average price: $75
Rating: 91

See Review

Starlight Distillery Orchard Blossom

This is an example where so much ridiculousness is promised on the label that you know the distillery must have figured something out. In this case, the well-regarded Indiana farm distillery finishes two of their different rye mash bills in barrels previously filled with Hampden Jamaican rum; honey; and peach flavored whiskey. Well OK! Designed to taste like the family’s “orchard in bloom,” this has an insane, estery rum funk on the nose and a palate that is fruity and bright. The most sui generis rye in our entire tasting and one of the better, more interesting spirits we’ve had this year.

Average price: $78
Rating: 95

See Review

Lost Lantern Wild Woodland George Dickel

While independent bottler Lost Lantern usually only deals in off-the-beaten-path craft distilleries, their newest collection is exclusively devoted to this Diageo-owned Tennessee whiskey brand. This release is a marriage of five Tennessee straight rye casks aged for seven years — in fact, it’s the first time George Dickel’s Tennessee-distilled rye has been offered as a stand-alone release. It’s an herbal and spicy rye, with hints of Andes chocolate mints, dill, allspice, cloves, with an oaky finish. Interesting, delicious stuff at a fair price in limited quantities (just 664 bottles).

Average price: $80
Rating: 94

See Review

Pursuit United Barrel Proof Rye

You can find another career after content creation! This growing brand created by hosts of the popular “Bourbon Pursuit” podcast Ryan Cecil and Kenny Coleman shows their ability to identify quality whiskey. An uncut and unfiltered blend of three different mash bills from two distilleries (Bardstown Bourbon Co. and Maryland’s Sagamore Spirit), there’s a distinct s’mores note on the nose. The palate is likewise dessert, with notes of meringue, lemon bars, and caramelized sugar, all balanced by wintry spices like nutmeg and cloves.

Average price: $80
Rating: 92

See Review

Hvenus Rye Whisky

Rye whiskey need not be strictly American and this Swedish distillate shows where other countries can take the spirit. An exacting mash bill of 78.6 percent rye, 11.9 percent wheat, 4.8 percent corn and 4.8 percent barley is aged in American oak for three to six years. It’s creamy and nutty on the palate, but there is an underlying rye graininess that is not quite as punishing and spicy as its U.S. counterparts. A fun international entrant to shake up the category.

Average price: $86
Rating: 91

See Review

Tamworth Distilling Chocorua Straight Rye Whiskey Aged 8 Years

Coming from New Hampshire’s avant-garde “wilderness-to-glass” distillery, Chocorua is a 100 percent rye made from a single crop of organic Maine-grown rye. This is distinctly a rye-forward whiskey — you can really taste the grains and the land and there’s a ton of peppery and gingery zip to it. Unlike their more standard no-age statement release, this 8-year-old has better barrel balance, with notes of chocolate-dipped cherries and caramel syrup.

Average price: $95
Rating: 90

See Review

The Best Rye Whiskeys Over $100

High West A Midwinter Night’s Dram Act 14

Once one of the more coveted yearly “LEs” in American rye — back at about Act 3 or so — this Utah distillery’s annual port barrel-finished rye release may have lost some of the online buzz, but it remains every bit as good as it always was. Act 14 celebrates the distillery’s 20th anniversary and adds Amontillado, Oloroso, and Pedro Ximénez sherry cask finishing to the signature Ruby and Tawny port finishing. The nose offers fresh strawberries and blackberries, while the palate leans more toward dark fruit preserves, coffee and mint, and a certain nuttiness. A complex after-dinner dram.

Average price: $125
Rating: 93

See Review

Booker’s The Reserves 2026

If the initial 2016 edition of Booker’s Rye is one of the most acclaimed American whiskey releases of the 21st century (with a secondary market price now to match!), this second ever rye release from the Jim Beam high proof label won’t quite reach that stratosphere. But it’s still worth your time. This is six year old straight rye finished in apple brandy barrels and infused with cinnamon. “Why?!!!!!!” yells the taters and, yes, you may presume the finishes were done to elevate whiskey that wasn’t turning out so well. Whatever the case, this Booker’s “Fireball” as some are derisively calling it is just what it claims to be: cinnamon spicy, apple pie with vanilla ice cream and a caramel drizzle, and a deep, oaky finish.

Average price: $130
Rating: 92

See Review

Lasso Motel Whiskey X James Dean 13-Year Rye Whiskey

Though it sure sounded like a gimmick — dead celebrity whiskey?! — this high-end release ended up being one of the better ryes of the entire year. I suppose it shouldn’t have been a surprise: this is classic 95/5 Indiana rye aged for 13 years, a level of maturity we rarely get to taste from MGP any more. With burnt sugar and cinnamon spice on the nose, the palate is packed with rich dark fruits, cherrywood, milk chocolate, and soft finish despite the 112 proof.

Average price: $150
Rating: 95

FAQs

Is rye whiskey smoother than bourbon?

Since rye is best known for its so-called spice notes (think: cinnamon, allspice, nutmeg, clove, and pepper), it’s often perceived as less “smooth” than bourbon, which uses a higher proportion of corn (and often wheat) in its mash bill, typically rendering it sweeter tasting.

Words like “terroir” and modifiers like “estate-grown” are usually associated with wine. Both of which contribute and refer to a sense of place — when producers celebrate where a wine comes from and all of the environmental factors at play, you can almost taste it in the final product.

A sense of place has long been overlooked in the world of spirits, particularly whiskey. But some American distillers, such as master distiller at Minden Mill Distillery Joe O’Sullivan, are trumpeting the seemingly small — yet massively impactful — artisanal practices that shape the flavor of their whiskey. From growing grains onsite to the small decisions made in the stillhouse, Joe champions an intentional approach to whiskey making at Minden Mill.

Today on the “VinePair Podcast,” Joe joins Zach to discuss the many aspects of their distinctive estate whiskey program. From why the Carson River Valley in Nevada’s high desert is a dynamic place for growing grain to the opportunities and challenges of the distilling process, the conversation looks at how forward-thinking and dynamic producers are pushing American whiskey forward in a variety of categories.

content:
On Tuesday Constellation Brands announced its acquisition of SpikedAde, one of the leading ready-to-drink (RTD) beverages in the growing boozy sports drink segment. Constellation agreed to a payment of $75 million for 100 percent ownership of the fast-growing brand, though payments in the next five years could reach up to an additional $278 million contingent on performance.

The acquisition marks Constellation Brands’s first foray into hard sports drinks — a growing segment within the already expanding category of spirit-based ready-to-drink beverages. SpikedAde is the runner-up to “Ade” segment leader Super Lyte, which boasts 65 percent share of off-premise sales, according to Brewbound.

Chief executive officer Jason Cohen founded SpikedAde in New Jersey in 2025. It packages non-carbonated, vodka-based drinks with Gatorade-like flavors, such as Electric Orange and Electric Blue, into 12-ounce cans. Cohen claimed he raised $10 million in the first two weeks of this year alone to expand the brand outside of New Jersey.

Now, SpikedAde is ranked among the top 25 RTD brands, according to NielsenIQ data. And though SpikeAde’s presence now extends along the East Coast, Constellation’s pickup will bring the brand to markets nationwide.

“With Constellation’s scale and expertise behind it, we’re excited to see SpikedAde reach even more consumers with its distinctive positioning and continue its remarkable growth trajectory,” Cohen states in a press release issued by Constellation.

The “Ade” category has exploded this past year. With Super Lyte, SpikedAde, and Vodkade leading the charge, the segment burst past the one million case mark this year, according to NielsenIQ data. With better-for-you and health-conscious trends swarming the market, new and established alcohol brands are leaning into sports marketing and functional ingredients like protein and electrolytes. And SpikedAde fits the bill, touting a zero-sugar, 100-calorie liquid.

“As consumer preferences evolve and new occasions continue to emerge, we’re excited to build on the strong foundation the SpikedAde team has created,” Constellation president and CEO Nicholas Fink says in the release.
